classification.difficultyReason: Follow explicit ruler and set-square instructions to construct perpendicular sides and measure the hypotenuse.

questions.mappingNote: The closest supplied skill is perpendicular-lines because constructing AC perpendicular to AB is central. Length measurement is a secondary prerequisite; the source has not yet stated Pythagoras’ theorem.
questions.methodNote: Use the printed ruler and set-square construction, join the remaining vertices and measure the hypotenuse. Do not replace this introductory measurement activity with an application of the algebraic theorem.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Follow explicit ruler and set-square instructions to construct perpendicular sides and measure the hypotenuse.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow explicit instructions to construct perpendicular segments, join their endpoints and measure; the expected length and enlargement explanation are supplied.

questions.mappingNote: The closest supplied skill is recognising perpendicular lines, applied through a set-square construction. Measurement is secondary; calculation using Pythagoras’ theorem is not the requested method.
questions.methodNote: The preceding construction specifies a horizontal base, a perpendicular segment above it drawn with a set square, joining the remaining endpoints and measuring the hypotenuse. This exercise repeats that method with lengths 8 cm and 6 cm; enlargement explains the supplied result.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct perpendicular segments of specified lengths and measure the third side using the printed construction method.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct evaluation of positive integer squares.

questions.mappingNote: The task assesses evaluating index notation directly, without applying Pythagoras’ theorem.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 pairs lengths with their squares; examples evaluate integer squares. Original prerequisite instruction for evaluating powers is unavailable.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct evaluation of positive integer squares.

classification.difficultyReason: Recall square roots of positive perfect squares.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses square roots of perfect squares.
questions.methodNote: Example 1 explicitly instructs taking a square root to recover a length from its square; Examples 2–3 use the same inverse relationship. Original prerequisite square-root teaching is unavailable.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recall square roots of positive perfect squares.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate two squares before adding or subtracting.

questions.mappingNote: Evaluating sums and differences containing indices is the most advanced directly assessed skill; no triangle or unknown side is requested.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1–3 evaluate each square before combining numerical terms. Example 3 uses exactly 7 squared plus 24 squared; Example 2 uses exactly 9 squared plus 12 squared. Original prerequisite teaching for powers and operation order is unavailable.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate two squares before adding or subtracting.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the hypotenuse opposite each marked right angle, then apply the stated sum-of-squares method and take its square root; rotations do not change the procedure.

questions.mappingNote: Each of 4a–f directly uses this method; rotation changes the hypotenuse’s position but not the calculation.
questions.methodNote: Examples 1 and 2 identify x as the hypotenuse, substitute the two shorter sides into Pythagoras’ theorem, evaluate their squares and sum, then take the positive square root.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the hypotenuse in differently oriented right triangles and apply Pythagoras’ theorem once.

classification.difficultyReason: Follow the supplied calculation columns and completed first row, then compare successive side lengths to describe their constant increases.

questions.mappingNote: Question 5 explicitly scaffolds those same calculations in columns a², b², c² and c, then asks students to identify the increases between rows.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 states a²+b²=c² and demonstrates squaring the two shorter sides, adding and taking the square root. Pages 4–5 supply a geometric justification and further hypotenuse examples.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete a scaffolded hypotenuse table using whole-number squares and recognise the repeated increases.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete repeated Pythagoras calculations in a table and identify a numerical pattern.

questions.mappingNote: Question 6 applies the same hypotenuse calculation to five rows, retaining separate columns for the squares, their sum and its square root, then asks for the resulting pattern.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 states a²+b²=c² and demonstrates squaring the two shorter sides, adding and taking a square root. Example 2 on pages 4–5 repeats this method for a rotated triangle.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Complete repeated Pythagoras calculations in a table and identify a numerical pattern.

classification.difficultyReason: Select right triangles within composite diagrams, transfer and combine horizontal or vertical lengths, and order successive Pythagorean calculations when one unknown supplies a later leg.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly applies the rectangle-diagonal method; b uses two right triangles sharing an altitude; c uses the rectangular strip to transfer a horizontal length; d sums base segments; e transfers lengths through the perpendicular scaffold; f applies the same hypotenuse calculation successively. No shorter-side rearrangement is required.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 states Pythagoras’ theorem and demonstrates substitution, squaring, addition and a final square root. Page 5 Example 3 identifies the right triangle formed by a rectangle’s diagonal.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify right triangles in composite diagrams and use supplied or derived perpendicular lengths, including a chain of three calculations.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the hypotenuse from each right-angle mark and apply the taught shorter-side procedure by subtracting squared lengths and taking the positive root.

questions.mappingNote: Each part gives a marked right angle, a hypotenuse and one leg, and asks for the other leg. This directly assesses the method of Example 4.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 states Pythagoras’ theorem. Example 4 on page 7 substitutes into the sum-of-squares equation, evaluates squares, subtracts the known leg’s square, and takes the positive square root. Page 8 reinforces this shorter-side method. Page 9’s converse example has printed errors and is not used for these solutions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply Pythagoras’ theorem to find a shorter side in three explicitly right-angled triangles.

classification.difficultyReason: Represent the rectangle's diagonal and sides as a right triangle, identify the diagonal as hypotenuse and use the routine shorter-side calculation.

questions.mappingNote: The question explicitly references Example 5 and assesses the same rectangle-side method, with a 20 cm side and 25 cm diagonal.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 states Pythagoras' theorem. Page 5 identifies a rectangle's diagonal as the hypotenuse. Page 8 Example 5 writes the sum-of-squares equation, substitutes the squares, subtracts the known square and takes the positive square root to obtain a rectangle's missing side.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the rectangle's diagonal as the hypotenuse and find the other side using one application of Pythagoras' theorem.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the longest side, compare its square with the other two squared lengths and, when equal, name the angle opposite that side.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly applies the converse, rather than finding an unknown side; the vertex opposite the longest side determines the named right angle.
questions.methodNote: Page 9 teaches comparing the square of the longest side with the sum of the other two squares, then naming the angle opposite the longest side when equal. Its Example 6 has two printed errors: the introductory formula reverses the stated longest-side role, and solution b prints 6 squared instead of 36 squared. The worked solutions here follow the correct verbal theorem and numerical comparisons. Pages 3 and 5 establish the sum-of-squares calculation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Compare squared side lengths and identify the angle opposite the longest side when equality holds.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the rectangle's diagonal as the hypotenuse and apply Pythagoras' theorem to the given side lengths.

questions.mappingNote: This practical rectangle problem directly assesses finding a diagonal using the method demonstrated in Example 3.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 states Pythagoras’ theorem and demonstrates squaring the two shorter sides, adding, then taking the positive square root. Page 5 Example 3 applies that method to a rectangle's diagonal.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the rectangle's diagonal as the hypotenuse and apply Pythagoras' theorem to the given side lengths.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the ladder as the hypotenuse and calculate the horizontal distance in a practical right-triangle problem.

questions.mappingNote: The wall and level ground form the right angle, so the ladder is the hypotenuse and the requested ground distance is a shorter side. The unrelated printed errors in page 9 Example 6 are not used.
questions.methodNote: Use Pythagoras’ theorem, substitute the hypotenuse and known shorter side, subtract their squared values, then take the positive square root, following Example 4 on page 7 and Example 5 on page 8.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the ladder as the hypotenuse and calculate the horizontal distance in a practical right-triangle problem.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret the equal cable lengths, calculate the attachment height using Pythagoras’ theorem, then include the flag’s vertical dimension.

questions.methodNote: Pages 7–8 demonstrate identifying the hypotenuse, substituting into Pythagoras’ theorem, subtracting the known square and taking the positive square root. questions.mappingNote: Each part directly applies the converse, rather than finding an unknown side. Pages 3 and 5 establish squared-side calculations; pages 7 and 8 provide shorter-side context.
